chapter_title: A Friend Found in Music (Twin Melodies)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 3 periods = 150 minutes
Total: 3 periods · 2h 30min

periods.activity_title: Reading the Poem and Unpacking Its Metaphors

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.194): paired share — favourite music, musician, reasons
Reading for Appreciation (p.195): figure of speech, metaphors-to-similes, rhyme scheme, anaphora, message, mood, speaker evidence

homework.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.195): poet's diary fill-in-the-blanks — eight gaps from the poem

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud with students following in their textbooks (p.194–195); a brief second read-along invites students to attend to the anaphoric 'Music is…' pattern and the ABCB rhyme.

Reflect and Respond (p.194): students spend a quick paired exchange answering what kind of music they prefer, who their favourite musician is, and giving reasons; two or three pairs share with the class.

Reading for Appreciation (p.195): teacher guides close-reading through all seven sub-questions — identifying the figure of speech in 'moves me', converting metaphors to similes, analysing the ABCB rhyme scheme and its impact, the purpose of anaphoric repetition, the poem's message, its mood, and evidence that the speaker is the poet herself; students discuss in pairs and then share with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's central device is the sustained series of 'Music is…' metaphors — ocean, rhythm, therapy, needed friend — each mapping onto an emotional state; keep the appreciation questions anchored to these specific metaphors rather than drifting into general comments on music. Students often conflate the mood question (the poem is warmly affirmative and intimate, not nostalgic) with theme; prompt them to distinguish feeling-tone from subject. The poet's diary fill-in task is set as take-home reinforcement so classroom time can go to the richer analytical appreciation questions.

periods.activity_title: Listening to a Santoor Story and Role-Playing Music's Value

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.199): pre-listen prediction — six multiple-choice questions on the conversation
Listen and Respond (p.199): listen, verify predictions, class discussion (transcript p.270)
Speaking Activity (p.200): four-role role play — music teacher, two students, parent debating music vs. studies

time_bands.activity: Listen and Respond — pre-listening (p.199): students read the six prediction questions silently and record their best guesses before hearing the conversation; teacher does not reveal answers at this stage.

Teacher reads the transcript aloud (a mother and Jaspreet at the music centre discussing his santoor practice problem and the plan to borrow an instrument); students check and correct their prediction answers, then discuss as a class which guesses were accurate and why the conversation unfolded as it did.

Speaking Activity (p.200): groups of four assign roles — music teacher, two students with contrasting views, parent — and rehearse briefly before presenting the role play; teacher prompts groups to frame responses in complete sentences and use logical continuity cues, then facilitates a brief whole-class reflection on the arguments made.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript involves Jaspreet's concern that the santoor teacher visits only twice a week, making home practice difficult, and his mother's solution of borrowing a friend's instrument; comprehension questions should be verified against these specific plot details. In the role play, the two student roles are deliberately contrasting — one sees music class as competing with study time, the other is convinced music is manageable and beneficial — so push groups to bring out that contrast rather than collapsing both students into agreement. Students who finish the role play quickly can be asked to swap roles and run a second round.
materials: Transcript text (Unit 6, p.270 of transcript booklet)

periods.activity_title: Phrasal Verbs in Context and Drafting an Invitation Letter

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary in Context (p.197): classify emotion words, fill blanks with nostalgia/elation/anguish/melancholy/jubilant
Vocabulary in Context (p.198): match six 'move'-based phrasal verbs to their meanings
Writing Task (p.201): draft a warm invitation letter to grandparents for a World Music Day sitar recital

homework.task_brief: Vocabulary in Context (p.198): create phrasal verbs from 'put', 'get', 'look', 'break'; find meanings and write sentences

time_bands.activity: Vocabulary in Context (p.197–198): teacher introduces the positive/negative emotion words from the poem ('feel blue', 'lifts my spirits', 'most cheerful'), students classify them and then choose the correct contextual word for the four fill-in sentences; teacher then presents the 'pull through' and 'moves me' examples from the poem to establish what phrasal verbs are, after which students individually match the six 'move' phrasal verb sentences to their meanings and verify as a class.

Writing Task (p.201): teacher models the required format on the board — sender's address, date, salutation, body paragraphs, complimentary close — and discusses the warm, personalised register expected; students then draft their own invitation letter to their grandparents for the World Music Day sitar recital, including the event's date, time, and venue, and complete a peer-response exchange before a final brief revision.

periods.teacher_notes: The vocabulary task is anchored in the poem's own emotional vocabulary — 'feel blue' (sadness) and 'lifts my spirits' (happiness) — so draw that connection explicitly before moving to the extended emotion-word set. The invitation letter requires switching between first person ('I am performing') and inclusive second person ('We invite you'); students regularly collapse both into 'I', so flag this in the model on the board. The phrasal verb creation task (put, get, look, break) is set for independent follow-up so that the full writing draft can be completed and peer-reviewed within the sitting.

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, tone, and the poet's purpose using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Metaphors of ocean, rhythm, therapy, and friend portraying music as emotional sustenance.
items.item_stem: In the poem, the speaker compares music to an ocean, a rhythm, a therapy, and a needed friend. Which of the following best describes what all four comparisons have in common?

options.label: A
options.text: They show music as something the speaker has recently discovered.

options.label: B
options.text: They present music as an indispensable force that sustains the speaker emotionally.

options.label: C
options.text: They suggest that music is enjoyable only during cheerful moments.

options.label: D
options.text: They indicate the speaker prefers music to human companionship.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have read 'pulls me to the shore' as novelty rather than irresistible pull.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have focused only on the stanza about cheerful times, missing the therapy and friend stanzas.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have over-read 'when no one seems to care' as rejection of people rather than music filling a gap.

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, tone, and the poet's purpose using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Metaphors of ocean, rhythm, therapy, and friend portraying music as emotional sustenance.
items.item_stem:
Read the second stanza on p.195, beginning “Music is the therapy”.

(i) What does the phrase ‘feel blue’ tell us about the speaker’s emotional state, and how does the metaphor of ‘therapy’ extend that idea?
(ii) The repetition of ‘Music is…’ across all three stanzas has been called anaphora. Evaluate how this device shapes the poem’s overall tone and reinforces its central argument.
items.visual_stimulus: Read the second stanza on p.195, beginning “Music is the therapy”.

expected_elements: 'Feel blue' signals sadness or low spirits in the speaker.
'Therapy' frames music as a curative or healing force, not entertainment.
Anaphora creates a meditative, incantatory rhythm reinforcing conviction.
Repetition cumulatively builds the argument that music is always present.
Tone is warmly affirmative; anaphora prevents the poem from sounding desperate.

items.source_lo: Student listens critically to a conversation and verifies predictions against heard details using audio-text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Jaspreet's dilemma over irregular santoor lessons and his mother's solution to borrow an instrument.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the conversation at the music centre. State whether each of the following statements is true or false, and give a one-sentence reason from the conversation for each verdict.
(1) Jaspreet is upset because the santoor is too difficult an instrument to learn.
(2) Watching videos of the santoor being played did not help Jaspreet improve.
(3) Jaspreet’s mother arranges for him to borrow a santoor from a friend.

options.text: Jaspreet is upset because the santoor is too difficult an instrument to learn.
Watching videos of the santoor being played did not help Jaspreet improve.
Jaspreet’s mother arranges for him to borrow a santoor from a friend.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (1) False — Jaspreet is upset because the teacher visits the centre only twice a week, making regular practice difficult. (2) True — Jaspreet explains that playing is a hands-on skill and watching videos did not substitute for actual practice. (3) True — his mother says she has a friend who used to play the santoor and can lend the instrument so Jaspreet may practise at home.

items.source_lo: Student listens critically to a conversation and verifies predictions against heard details using audio-text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Jaspreet's dilemma over irregular santoor lessons and his mother's solution to borrow an instrument.
items.item_stem: After listening to the conversation between Jaspreet and his mother, reflect on the following: Jaspreet says that watching videos of the santoor ‘did not help’ because playing is a hands-on skill. Do you agree that learning a musical instrument cannot be supported by watching others play it? Give at least two reasons for your view, drawing on what you heard in the conversation.

expected_elements: Acknowledges Jaspreet’s specific argument that playing is hands-on.
Offers a reasoned personal stance, not a bare assertion.
Draws at least one detail from the conversation to support the view.
Considers a counter-view or limitation of the position taken.

items.source_lo: Student argues a position with rationale and responds impromptu using role play as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four-role debate on whether music classes are worth the time — teacher, two students, parent.
items.item_stem: You are Student 2 in the role play — a learner who is convinced that taking music classes is worthwhile and does not harm studies. In two to three sentences, describe your experience of balancing music practice with schoolwork and explain why you would encourage Student 1 to continue.

expected_elements: Speaks in role as a music learner who manages time effectively.
Gives at least one concrete reason music is beneficial rather than a distraction.
Uses complete sentences and addresses Student 1 directly.
Maintains a persuasive but respectful tone throughout.

items.source_lo: Student argues a position with rationale and responds impromptu using role play as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four-role debate on whether music classes are worth the time — teacher, two students, parent.
items.item_stem: The music teacher in the role play argues that learning an instrument builds discipline and emotional resilience. Do you agree or disagree with this view? Present your argument in a brief impromptu speech of three to four sentences, giving at least one reason and one piece of evidence or example to support your position.

expected_elements: States a clear agree or disagree position at the outset.
Provides at least one logical reason backed by an example or evidence.
Anticipates and briefly addresses an opposing view.
Speaks fluently in complete sentences with a reasoned conclusion.

items.source_lo: Student drafts a transactional letter in an appropriate register using functional writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: An appeal to a school principal to introduce an after-school music appreciation club.
items.item_stem: Your school does not currently have a music club. Write a formal letter to your school principal requesting the establishment of an after-school music appreciation club. Include: why such a club would benefit students emotionally and academically; what activities the club could offer; and a polite request for the principal’s approval. Use the correct formal letter format with sender’s address, date, salutation, body, and complimentary close.

expected_elements: Uses correct formal letter format throughout.
States purpose clearly in the opening paragraph.
Gives two or more specific reasons for the club’s value.
Proposes at least one concrete activity the club would run.
Closes with a polite and appropriately formal request.

items.source_lo: Student drafts a transactional letter in an appropriate register using functional writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: An appeal to a school principal to introduce an after-school music appreciation club.
items.item_stem: A local newspaper has published an editorial arguing that school timetables are too crowded for arts subjects like music. Write a letter to the editor responding to this view. In your letter: acknowledge the concern about time; present a counter-argument for why music education deserves a place in the school day; and use at least one specific example to support your position. Use formal letter-to-editor format.

expected_elements: Uses formal letter-to-editor format correctly.
Acknowledges the opposing concern fairly before countering.
Builds a coherent argument for music education with a specific example.
Demonstrates a discursive register distinct from personal or informal writing.
Concludes with a clear, reasoned call to action or position.

items.source_context: Emotion vocabulary and 'move'-based phrasal verbs drawn from the poem's language.
items.item_stem: Match each emotion word in Column A with the feeling it most closely describes in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A | Column B |
|---|---|
| nostalgia | deep sadness and hopelessness |
| elation | longing for the past |
| melancholy | intense feeling of joy and triumph |
| anguish | great happiness and excitement |
| jubilant | a gentle, lingering sadness |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: nostalgia – longing for the past; elation – great happiness and excitement; melancholy – a gentle, lingering sadness; anguish – deep sadness and hopelessness; jubilant – intense feeling of joy and triumph.

answer_key.right: intense feeling of joy and triumph

items.source_lo: Student identifies and uses phrasal verbs and emotion-related vocabulary in context using grammar-in-writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Emotion vocabulary and 'move'-based phrasal verbs drawn from the poem's language.
items.item_stem:
The poem uses the phrasal verb 'pull through' to mean succeeding despite difficulty, and 'moves me' to mean stirring someone emotionally. Read the following sentences about musicians and music learners. Replace the underlined word or phrase in each sentence with the correct phrasal verb from the box (move on, move in, move out, move along) and rewrite the sentence.

1. After years at the same music school, Riya decided to progress to a more advanced conservatoire.
2. The new piano arrived and the family had to vacate the small study to make room for it.
3. The street performer asked the gathering crowd to keep walking so the pavement stayed clear.
4. A young vocalist joined the music centre last week and has settled into her practice room.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. After years at the same music school, Riya decided to move on to a more advanced conservatoire. 2. The new piano arrived and the family had to move out of the small study to make room for it. 3. The street performer asked the gathering crowd to move along so the pavement stayed clear. 4. A young vocalist moved in to the music centre last week and has settled into her practice room.
